title: What is ISO 45001 and who needs it?
excerpt: What ISO 45001 is, which organisations are asked for it and by whom, what the certificate proves, and how to start — written for the manager who has just been asked for it.
introduction: The request usually arrives in a pre-qualification questionnaire or a framework application: "Please provide evidence of your occupational health and safety management system, e.g. ISO 45001 certification." For a contractor, a manufacturer, a logistics operator or a facilities provider it is the moment the question stops being "should we" and becomes "how, and by when". This guide explains what ISO 45001 is, who asks for it, what a certificate proves and does not, and how to begin, without assuming that you have read the standard.

body: What is ISO 45001?

ISO 45001:2018 is the international standard for an occupational health and safety (OH&S) management system. It sets out what an organisation must have in place to identify the hazards its work creates, assess and control the risks to workers and others, comply with the law that applies to it, involve workers in the process, respond to incidents and emergencies, and improve its performance over time. It follows the same structure as ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, so an organisation that holds either will recognise the shape: context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement. It is the standard that replaced OHSAS 18001 and it is the only OH&S management system standard that is recognised internationally. The 2018 edition is current; a revision is in development but has not been published, and certification continues to the 2018 edition.

The standard does not tell an organisation how safe it must be; that is the job of the law. It requires the organisation to build and run a system that finds its own hazards, sets its own controls and checks that they work. This is why it applies equally to a demolition contractor and a call centre: the hazards differ, the system does not.
Who needs ISO 45001?

Any organisation whose work can hurt someone, which is every organisation, can implement ISO 45001. Certification is sought when someone asks for it or when the consequences of failure are severe. The parties that ask are, in rough order of frequency: principal contractors and their frameworks, which name ISO 45001 as the accepted evidence of a health and safety management system at pre-qualification; public-sector buyers and infrastructure owners, whose tender questions on health and safety are answered in one line by a certificate; large manufacturers and energy operators, whose vendor registration portals require it of suppliers working on their sites; insurers, who underwrite employers' liability and contractors' cover on the strength of the system behind the claims record; and, increasingly, the organisation's own board, for whom a certified system is the evidence that the duty of care has been discharged.

By sector, the holders are construction and civil engineering, manufacturing and heavy industry, energy, oil and gas, utilities, transport and logistics, facilities management, waste and recycling, mining, and any organisation with lone workers, driving, working at height, machinery, chemicals or public interaction. Globally, 542,527 ISO 45001 certificates covering 941,546 sites were recorded in the 2024 survey of certificates, the third most widely held management system standard after ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. The scale of what it addresses is larger still: an estimated 2.9 million work-related deaths a year worldwide, most of them from occupational disease rather than accidents (2023 estimate), which is why the standard treats health as seriously as safety.
What the certificate proves

A certificate issued by an independent, accredited certification body states that, on the dates audited, the organisation operated an OH&S management system conforming to ISO 45001 within the scope stated on the certificate. A buyer can rely on that: the hazards have been identified, the risks assessed and controlled, legal requirements identified and checked, workers consulted, incidents investigated, and management reviewing the results. The certificate is maintained by annual surveillance audits and renewed every three years, so it is a statement about a working system rather than a single inspection.

It does not prove that no accident will happen, that every site was inspected, or that the organisation is compliant with every law on every day. Buyers who need assurance about a particular site or activity use the certificate as the baseline and add their own site inspection or audit; the two are complementary.
How ISO 45001 certification works

Certification follows the same route as every management system standard, described in full on the certification process page. After a quotation based on headcount, sites and risk, a Stage 1 audit reviews the documented system and the organisation's readiness; a Stage 2 audit, normally two to eight weeks later, tests the system in operation across the scope, on site; an independent decision issues the certificate for three years; annual surveillance audits sample the system; and recertification in year three renews it. For an organisation of 50 to 250 people on one or two sites the audits take a few days each, and the whole route from application to certificate is commonly three to five months when the system is already running. Organisations holding a certificate with another body can transfer it to TRAIBCERT without repeating the initial audits.
Benefits of ISO 45001

The commercial benefit is access: pre-qualification questions that took a page are answered with a certificate number, and frameworks that require it are open. The regulatory benefit is a system that identifies the law that applies and checks compliance on a schedule, which is what an enforcing authority expects to see after an incident. The operational benefit is fewer incidents and less lost time, because hazards are found and controlled before they cause harm, and near misses are recorded and acted on rather than forgotten; organisations that certify typically report a measurable fall in lost-time incident rates in the first two cycles, although the mechanism is the system, not the certificate. The reputational benefit is the one the board notices: a fatality or serious injury without a demonstrable management system behind the controls is a corporate failing as well as a human one, and a certified system is the evidence that the organisation took the duty seriously.
ISO 45001 and safety scheme memberships

In the UK construction supply chain, contractors are often members of health and safety pre-qualification schemes and ask whether ISO 45001 is still needed. The two are different things: scheme membership evidences that the contractor's arrangements met a questionnaire at a point in time; ISO 45001 certifies the management system behind those arrangements, audited annually on site. Principal contractors increasingly specify ISO 45001 for higher-risk packages and accept scheme membership for lower-risk ones. Holding both is common, and a certified system makes the annual scheme renewal largely a matter of uploading existing records.
Getting started with ISO 45001

Start by deciding the scope: which sites, activities and workers the system will cover, written as a buyer would read it. Then assess the gap between what you have and what the standard requires, using the readiness checklist; most organisations already have risk assessments, method statements, training records and incident reports, and the gap is usually in worker consultation, legal compliance evaluation, objectives and management review. Give the work an owner with time, and train two or three people as internal auditors so that the system is checked before TRAIBCERT checks it. If you also hold ISO 9001 or ISO 14001, build one integrated system and audit it once; the common structure is designed for this.
Frequently asked questions

Is ISO 45001 a legal requirement? No. Health and safety law applies regardless; ISO 45001 is voluntary and is a way of managing compliance and being able to prove it. Contracts and frameworks may make it a condition.
How long does certification take? Three to five months from application when the system is already operating; longer if it is being built. The audits themselves take days, not weeks.

How much does it cost? The audit fee depends on headcount, sites and the risk of the activities; TRAIBCERT quotes a fixed price for the three-year cycle in advance. The larger cost is usually internal time.

Can a small contractor be certified? Yes. The system scales to the organisation; a twelve-person contractor's system is a few procedures, site records and a management review, and the audit is priced for the size of the business.

Does ISO 45001 cover subcontractors? The organisation must control the OH&S risks of work done on its behalf, so subcontractor selection, briefing and monitoring are within the system; the subcontractors themselves are not certified by your certificate.
What replaced OHSAS 18001? ISO 45001 did, in 2018; OHSAS 18001 certificates are no longer valid.
Can it be combined with ISO 9001 and ISO 14001? Yes, and most holders do: one integrated system, one internal audit programme, one combined certification visit.
What to do next

Download the ISO 45001 readiness checklist and use it to find your gaps, then read the ISO 45001 certification page for scope, timeline and how to request a quotation. If you already hold a certificate elsewhere, the certificate transfer page explains what is needed.

title: ISO 9001:2026 is published: a practical transition checklist
excerpt: The revision is no longer anticipated; it is published. Here is how to plan a calm, staged transition inside your existing certification cycle.
introduction: ISO 9001:2026 was published on 16 September 2026, replacing the 2015 edition that most certified organisations have run for a decade. Every revision of a management system standard produces the same pattern: a long quiet period, then a rush as the transition deadline approaches, and a surveillance visit at which nobody can explain what changed. Organisations that treat the transition as a planned project inside their normal certification cycle spend less on it and get more from it. This checklist is that project.

supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit, an independent certification decision and a three-year certificate with annual surveillance. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.
supportButtons: Buttons: Get a certification quote (/certification/iso-9001) · Talk to a specialist
body: 1. Know your dates

Transition arrangements give certified organisations a fixed window from publication in which to move to the new edition; after it closes, certificates to ISO 9001:2015 are no longer valid. Your window is bounded by two things: the published transition timetable, which is set out with a timeline on TRAIBCERT's ISO 9001 page, and your own surveillance and recertification dates, because the transition audit is normally combined with a scheduled visit rather than booked as an extra. Put both on one calendar before anything else.
2. Read the changes, not the whole standard

The structure of the 2026 edition follows the harmonised structure used across management system standards, so the clause numbering you know is preserved. The substantive changes are concentrated in a few areas: the treatment of the organisation's context, including climate-related and other external factors; expectations on ethics and organisational culture; the handling of change and of risks and opportunities; and the use of technology, including automation and AI, within the quality management system. A one-page summary of the changes and where each touches your system is the first document to produce, because it converts a 40-page standard into a list of perhaps a dozen actions.
3. Run a gap assessment against your system, not against the text

The purpose of the gap assessment is a short list of the changes that affect your documented information, your risk approach, your internal audit programme and your management review inputs. It is not a perfect answer to every clause. Use your own process map as the frame: for each process, ask whether the 2026 changes alter what the process must consider, record or review. Most organisations find that the majority of the work is in context, planning and management review, and that operational processes need little change.
4. Give each gap an owner and a date inside the cycle

Map each gap to a process owner and a date that falls before your next scheduled audit. Fold the work into instruments you already run: add the new context factors to the next management review agenda; add the changed requirements to the next round of internal audits; update the risk register at its next scheduled review. A transition run this way is a set of small changes to existing routines rather than a separate programme with its own meetings.
5. Brief people before you brief the auditor

The most common transition failure at audit is not a missing document but a manager who cannot say what changed in their area. Awareness training for process owners is inexpensive and can be run in an hour; TRAIBCERT's Academy offers an updated ISO 9001 Awareness course for exactly this purpose. Brief your certification body at the same time, so the transition audit is planned with the right duration and the right auditor.
6. Decide when to be audited

Early transition has advantages: the audit can be combined with the next surveillance visit, the organisation is not competing for audit dates near the deadline, and tender responses can cite the current edition. Late transition has none, apart from delay. If your recertification falls in the first half of the window, transition at recertification; if it falls late, transition at a surveillance visit and do not wait.
What to do next

Download the ISO 9001 readiness checklist, updated for the 2026 edition, and read the transition section of the ISO 9001 certification page for the timetable TRAIBCERT applies. If your certificate is held with another body and you would prefer to transition with TRAIBCERT, the certificate transfer page explains what is needed; transfer and transition can be combined in one visit.

title: Cyber Essentials or ISO/IEC 27001: which one does your organisation need?
excerpt: One is a UK baseline of five technical controls; the other is an international management system. They answer different questions, and many organisations need both.
introduction: The question arrives in two forms. A UK organisation has been asked for Cyber Essentials by a public-sector buyer or an insurer and wonders whether ISO/IEC 27001 would be the better investment. An enterprise supplier holds ISO/IEC 27001 and has just been told that a UK contract requires Cyber Essentials as well. The answer to both is the same: the two schemes answer different questions, and holding one does not answer the other.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT certifies organisations to Cyber Essentials (UK)
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides assessment of the five technical controls by a licensed assessor, with the certificate issued on a pass. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.

body: What Cyber Essentials is

Cyber Essentials is a UK government-backed scheme that certifies five technical controls: firewalls and internet gateways, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection, and security update management, applied to the devices and cloud services in scope. At the basic level the organisation answers a question set and an assessor verifies the answers; at Cyber Essentials Plus an assessor tests the controls on a sample of devices and the external boundary. It is fast, inexpensive and specific. It is also a UK scheme: it is mandated in UK public procurement for contracts involving personal data or ICT, asked for by UK insurers, and unknown to most buyers elsewhere. An organisation with no UK customers or insurers has no reason to hold it.
What ISO/IEC 27001 is

ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard for an information security management system. It does not prescribe five controls; it requires the organisation to understand its context and its interested parties, assess information security risk, decide which controls apply from a reference set of ninety-three, operate them, measure them, audit them and improve them, under the direction of top management. Certification is by an independent, accredited certification body after a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit and is maintained by annual surveillance. Enterprise buyers, regulated clients and international customers ask for it because a certificate tells them that security is governed, not only configured.
Effort, cost and time

Cyber Essentials is measured in weeks and hundreds of pounds; Cyber Essentials Plus in weeks and low thousands. ISO/IEC 27001 is measured in months of implementation and an audit priced on the size and complexity of the organisation, followed by annual surveillance. The comparison is not like for like: the technical controls Cyber Essentials tests are a subset of what a well-run ISMS would select, and an organisation with a certified ISMS usually meets the Cyber Essentials controls already, but it must still be assessed against the scheme to hold the certificate, because a UK buyer asking for Cyber Essentials cannot accept an ISO certificate in its place.
Which contracts ask for which

In the UK: public-sector contracts involving personal data or ICT name Cyber Essentials, with Plus specified where the risk is higher; health-service and central-government suppliers are increasingly asked for Plus; insurers make the basic certificate a condition of cover. Everywhere: enterprise security questionnaires, regulated clients in finance and health, and international tenders ask for ISO/IEC 27001, and increasingly SOC 2 for cloud services sold to North American customers. Read the wording of what you have been asked for; it usually answers the question.
A sensible sequence

For a UK organisation starting from nothing: Cyber Essentials first, because it is fast, mandated and fixes the basics that cause most incidents; Plus when a contract requires it; ISO/IEC 27001 when enterprise or regulated customers ask, or when the organisation wants a governed system rather than a set of controls. For an organisation that already holds ISO/IEC 27001 and now sells into the UK public sector: add Cyber Essentials, which should be a formality if the ISMS is working. For an organisation with no UK footprint: ISO/IEC 27001 alone, and do not spend on a scheme your buyers will not recognise.
What to do next

If your next contract names a scheme, start there. If you are building long-term assurance, start with the risk assessment. TRAIBCERT certifies both: see the Cyber Essentials and ISO/IEC 27001 pages for scope, pricing and how to begin.

title: Building a carbon baseline that survives customer scrutiny
excerpt: Scope 3 is where most carbon inventories fall apart. A defensible boundary and a consistent method matter more than precision.
introduction: A carbon baseline is the year against which every later reduction claim is measured, and it is the number most often challenged by a customer's sustainability team, an investor's questionnaire or a public-sector buyer reading a carbon reduction plan. The challenges are rarely about arithmetic. They are about what was counted, how, and whether next year will be counted the same way. A baseline that answers those three questions survives scrutiny; one built for a quick disclosure does not.

supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a scoped engagement, a fixed price quoted in advance, and a report written to be relied on by the people who asked for it. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.

body: Fix the boundary first

The boundary decides which sites, entities and activities are inside the inventory. Choose the consolidation approach (operational control is the usual choice for a single organisation), list every site and legal entity with its treatment, and write down the exclusions with a reason. Most baseline disputes trace back to a boundary that was never written down: a leased warehouse that appeared in year two, a subsidiary that was in the accounts but not in the inventory, an outsourced fleet that nobody classified. The boundary document is one page and it is the most valuable page in the inventory.
Choose a method and keep it

Scope 1 and Scope 2 are largely a matter of collecting fuel, refrigerant and electricity data and applying published emission factors for the reporting year; the discipline is in recording which factor set was used, keeping the invoices and meter readings that support each figure, and reporting Scope 2 by both the location-based and market-based methods. Consistency matters more than precision: a baseline calculated with one factor set and a later year with another is not a reduction, it is a restatement, and a verifier will say so.
Scope 3: be selective and be honest about quality

Scope 3 is where inventories fall apart, because organisations either try to estimate all fifteen categories from spend data and produce a number nobody believes, or leave it out and produce a baseline nobody accepts. The defensible route is a screening exercise that identifies the categories that are material for the business (purchased goods and services, upstream transport, business travel, commuting, use of sold products, and investments are the usual candidates), a method for each material category with its data source and quality stated, and an explicit list of the categories excluded with the reason. A baseline that says "purchased goods estimated from spend with an average-data method, data quality low, improvement plan in place" is credible; a baseline with a precise Scope 3 figure and no method is not.
Document as if a verifier were coming, because one will

Customers and frameworks increasingly require independent verification of GHG inventories, and UK public contracts above the threshold require a carbon reduction plan with a baseline. Verification to the international standard for GHG verification examines exactly the things above: boundary, method, data, calculation and the statement. Keeping the evidence file as you build the baseline (boundary document, method statement, factor sources, activity data with its source, calculation workbook with version control, and the list of assumptions and exclusions) turns verification from an archaeological exercise into a review.
Re-baseline only for a reason

Write a re-baselining policy at the start: the baseline is recalculated when a structural change (acquisition, disposal, outsourcing), a method change or an error moves the figure by more than a stated threshold. Anything else is reported as a change in the current year. Without the policy, every improvement invites the accusation that the baseline was moved.
What to do next

If your baseline exists, request a readiness review before verification; if it does not, start with the boundary document and the screening of Scope 3. TRAIBCERT verifies GHG inventories, carbon neutrality and net-zero claims and carbon reduction plans, and the verification statement is what a customer or buyer can rely on.

title: How to run an internal audit programme people actually value
excerpt: Internal audits should surface risk, not paperwork. A few structural changes make the difference between a programme that is tolerated and one that is used.
introduction: Every management system standard requires internal audits, and in most organisations they are the least valued activity in the system: a calendar of clause-by-clause checks, performed by whoever is free, producing findings about missing signatures. The certification auditor sees the schedule, the reports and the closed actions, and the organisation sees a cost. It does not have to be so. An internal audit programme that is designed to find risk is one of the few controls that management asks for more of.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT trains teams through Training and auditing skills
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides Foundation, Awareness, Internal Auditor and Lead Auditor courses, self-paced on the Academy, tutor-led online or onsite. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.

body: Plan by risk, not by clause

The programme should audit what could hurt the organisation, in proportion to how much. Start the annual plan from three inputs: the risk register, the results of the last year (external findings, complaints, incidents, near misses, customer feedback), and change (new sites, new products, new people, new systems). A process that has had no change and no problems for three years can be audited lightly; a process that has just been reorganised deserves a full audit early. A plan built this way can be explained to management in one sentence per audit, which a clause-by-clause plan cannot.
Audit processes, across the standards

Audit the purchasing process once, against every standard the organisation holds, rather than auditing "clause 8.4" three times under three schemes. Process audits follow the work as it happens, from the input to the output, and find the problems that live at the boundaries between departments, which is where most problems live. They also produce one report the process owner can act on, instead of three that repeat each other.
Auditors need competence and independence, not seniority

The requirements are that auditors are competent and do not audit their own work. Competence means understanding auditing (how to plan, gather evidence, evaluate it and report), understanding the standard, and understanding enough of the process to ask a second question. A two-day Internal Auditor course covers the first two; pairing a trained auditor with a process expert from another department covers the third. Rotate auditors across processes, keep a small pool rather than a large one, and give them time in the plan: an audit squeezed into a spare afternoon produces the signature findings everyone dislikes.
Write findings that lead somewhere

A finding is useful when it states the evidence, the requirement and the gap in a way the process owner recognises, and when it is graded honestly: a systemic failure is not "an observation" because the manager is senior, and a missing date is not a major nonconformity. Every nonconformity should be followed by the root-cause question, and the corrective action should address the cause. Reports should be short, delivered within days, and discussed with the process owner before they are issued.
Close the loop, and show the result

Actions are verified, not merely marked complete; the verification is recorded; and the programme reports to management review in terms management uses: which risks were tested, what was found, what was fixed, and what it prevented. When management review starts asking for particular audits, the programme has become valuable.
What to do next

Download the internal audit plan template, which is risk-based by design, and consider Internal Auditor training for a small pool of auditors across the standards you hold. TRAIBCERT's Academy courses are available self-paced, tutor-led online, or onsite for a team.

title: Pre-shipment inspection: avoiding costly surprises at the port
excerpt: Once goods have shipped, your options narrow and your costs rise. Independent inspection moves the decision point earlier, to when the balance payment is still in your hands.
introduction: The container arrives, the cartons are opened, and the goods are short, damaged, mislabelled or simply not what was approved. From this point every option costs money: return freight, rework in the UK, a discount to move stock that cannot be sold at full price, a missed season. The supplier, paid in full, is unhurried. The buyer discovers that the leverage it had, the balance payment, was released against a photograph and an assurance.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT delivers Third-party inspection
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a scoped engagement, a fixed price quoted in advance, and a report written to be relied on by the people who asked for it. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.
supportButtons: Buttons: Get a quote (/certification/inspection) · Talk to a specialist
body: Move the decision point to the factory

A pre-shipment inspection puts an independent inspector in the factory when production is complete and at least 80% of the order is packed, before the balance payment is released. The inspector draws a random sample from across the cartons, checks it against the approved sample and the specification, tests function and safety on site, checks packaging, labelling, barcodes and shipping marks for the destination market, and sends a flash report the same day. The buyer releases payment on evidence or holds it with photographs in hand, and the supplier corrects the lot while it is still in the factory.
How the sample decides the result

Sampling follows the international standard for inspection by attributes at general inspection level II: an order of 5,000 units gives a sample of 200. The acceptable quality limit, agreed before the inspection, sets how many defects of each severity the sample may contain before the lot fails; the usual limits are zero critical defects, up to 2.5% major and up to 4.0% minor. The result is a rule applied to a random sample, which is why a supplier cannot argue with it and why a buyer can rely on it without inspecting every unit.
When one inspection is not enough

Pre-shipment inspection tells you what was made. For new suppliers, new products, long production runs and tight dates, two earlier points are worth buying: an initial production check when the first units come off the line, which catches wrong materials and mis-set tooling before thousands are made the same way, and a during-production inspection at 20 to 50% of the run, which finds systemic defects while the remaining 50 to 80% can still be made correctly. Container loading supervision closes the last gap, verifying that the goods inspected are the goods loaded, in the right quantity, stowed properly and sealed.
What it costs against what it prevents

Most consumer-goods pre-shipment inspections take one inspector day, quoted as a fixed fee in advance. The return is easiest to see in the returns rate: a few per cent of a container returned by customers erases the margin on the whole order, and a failed lot caught at the factory is reworked at the supplier's cost rather than the buyer's.
What to do next

Book pre-shipment inspection for any order where the balance payment is released against production completion, and add production and loading inspections for the orders that cannot go wrong. TRAIBCERT inspects in the UK, the Middle East and India and at supplier locations elsewhere through its inspector network, with the report issued by TRAIBCERT.

title: ISO/IEC 42001: first steps towards AI governance
excerpt: AI assurance questions are appearing in procurement. ISO/IEC 42001 gives you a structure to answer them, whether you build AI systems or only use them.
introduction: Security questionnaires now ask a new set of questions: which AI systems do you use, what data do they see, who is accountable for their outputs, how do you assess their risks and how would you know if one went wrong. Regulators in several jurisdictions are writing obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems, and buyers are asking for evidence before the law requires it. ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the international standard for an AI management system, is the structure most organisations are using to answer.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT certifies organisations to ISO/IEC 42001
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit, an independent certification decision and a three-year certificate with annual surveillance. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.
supportButtons: Buttons: Get a certification quote (/certification/iso-42001) · Talk to a specialist
body: It is a management system, and that is the point

ISO/IEC 42001 follows the harmonised structure shared by ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 27001: context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement, applied to the organisation's development, provision or use of AI. It adds what AI specifically needs: an AI policy and objectives, defined roles and accountability for AI systems, an AI risk assessment and an AI system impact assessment that considers individuals, groups and society, controls over the AI system life cycle and over data, and transparency to the people affected. An organisation that already holds ISO/IEC 27001 will recognise the machinery and can integrate the two.
You do not have to build AI to need it

The standard applies to organisations that use AI as much as to those that develop it. A professional services firm using generative tools on client material, a retailer using recommendation and pricing models, a recruiter using screening software, and a software company embedding third-party models in its product all make decisions with AI that affect people, and all are being asked how those decisions are governed. Scope the system to the AI you actually use and the roles you actually play (provider, deployer, or both), and the standard becomes proportionate.
Five first steps

Inventory: list every AI system in use or development, its purpose, its data, its supplier and its owner. Most organisations find more than they expected, and the list is the foundation of everything else.
Roles: decide who is accountable for AI at board level and who owns each system; write it down.
Risk and impact: for each system, assess the risks to the organisation and the impact on the people affected, in proportion to what the system decides; the high-impact systems get the attention.
Controls and life cycle: define how systems are specified, tested, approved, monitored and retired, and how data is governed, using the standard's reference controls as the menu.
Transparency and incidents: decide what people are told and how problems are reported, investigated and corrected.
What certification proves

Certification by an independent, accredited certification body tells a buyer or regulator that the AI management system exists, is operated and is audited, in the same way an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate does for security. It does not certify that a particular model is accurate or fair; it certifies that the organisation governs its AI in a way that would detect and correct a problem. That is the assurance procurement teams are asking for, and it is the assurance an AI-specific law will expect to see behind a conformity claim.
What to do next

Start with the inventory and the accountability decision; both cost nothing and both are asked about first. Download the ISO/IEC 42001 readiness checklist for the rest, and read the ISO/IEC 42001 certification page for scope, timeline and how it integrates with an existing ISO/IEC 27001 certificate.

title: Penetration test or vulnerability scan: what each finds and what each proves
excerpt: A scan lists known weaknesses; a penetration test shows what an attacker could do with them. Which one a customer, an insurer or a certification audit is asking for, and when you need both.
introduction: A customer questionnaire asks for "evidence of regular penetration testing"; the IT provider offers a monthly vulnerability scan report and says it amounts to the same thing. It does not, and the difference matters to the customer, to the insurer and to an information security audit. Both are useful and most organisations need both, but they answer different questions and are bought, priced and scheduled differently.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT delivers Penetration testing
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a scoped engagement, a fixed price quoted in advance, and a report written to be relied on by the people who asked for it. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.
supportButtons: Buttons: Get a quote (/certification/penetration-testing) · Talk to a specialist
body: What a vulnerability scan does

A vulnerability scan is an automated comparison of your systems against a database of known weaknesses: missing patches, outdated software versions, default configurations, open services, known-vulnerable components. It runs in hours, can be repeated weekly or monthly, covers every address in scope, and produces a list ranked by a severity score. Its strengths are breadth, repeatability and cost. Its limits are that it only finds what is already catalogued, that it cannot tell whether a weakness is actually exploitable in your environment, that it produces false positives that someone must triage, and that it knows nothing about the logic of your applications, your users or the way your systems are connected.
What a penetration test does

A penetration test is a time-boxed, authorised attempt by a skilled tester to achieve an objective an attacker would want: read customer data, take over an account, move from the public website into the internal network, escalate from a user to an administrator. The tester uses scanners, but also reads the application, chains low-severity findings into a high-impact path, tests business logic that no scanner understands, and stops at agreed boundaries. It takes days, is scoped to specific systems, and produces a report of what was achieved, how, with evidence, and what to fix first. Its strength is that it proves impact: a finding in a penetration test report is something a person actually did, not something a database says might be possible. Its limits are cost, scope and the fact that it is a point in time.
What each proves to the people asking

A customer or a framework asking for "penetration testing" wants to know that someone competent has tried to break in and reported what they found; a scan report does not answer that, and a procurement team that knows the difference will say so. An insurer usually wants both: scanning as evidence of ongoing hygiene and a test as evidence that the perimeter and the key applications have been examined. A certification audit against ISO/IEC 27001 looks for the organisation to have decided, on the basis of its risk assessment, what technical testing it needs and to have done it; for most organisations that decision is a regular scan plus an annual test of internet-facing systems and any application that handles sensitive data, with a re-test after significant change. In the UK, Cyber Essentials Plus includes a specific external vulnerability assessment as part of the scheme; it is not a penetration test and is not accepted as one.
How often, and of what

The pattern that satisfies most buyers and audits is monthly or continuous scanning of everything, annual penetration testing of internet-facing infrastructure and the applications that matter, a test of any new system or major change before it goes live, and re-testing of critical findings after they are fixed. Scope the test to the systems that hold the data your customers care about, agree the objectives in writing, and choose a tester whose report separates evidence from opinion and rates findings by exploitability as well as by severity.
What to do next

If you have scan reports and no test, an external infrastructure and web application test is the usual first engagement and the one most questionnaires are asking about. TRAIBCERT's penetration testing page describes the nine test types, how scoping works and what the report contains.

body: How to use it

Work through the sections with the people who run each process, recording the evidence you would show an auditor rather than what you believe is true; where the evidence does not exist, mark the question partial or not started and name an owner. The summary page counts the status by section and asks for three priorities. When most questions are in place and the remaining ones have owners and dates, the system is ready for Stage 1. Organisations moving from the 2015 edition can filter the workbook to the questions marked "2026" to see only what changed.
What it is not
The checklist is a self-assessment aid. It is not a statement of conformity, it does not replace the standard, and completing it does not affect the outcome of an audit.

title: Impartiality: why a certification body cannot consult on what it certifies
excerpt: A certification body that helped design your system could not audit it objectively. The rule, the reason, and what it means when you ask your certification body for advice.
introduction: Impartiality is the principle that a certification decision must be free of any interest in its outcome. The international standard that governs certification bodies requires each body to identify the threats to its impartiality, to manage them, and to keep certification separate from consultancy: a body may not certify a management system that it, or a related organisation, helped to design, document or implement, and it may not offer to make certification easier for those who buy its other services. Accreditation checks that the body actually does this. The rule exists because a certificate is only worth what an independent audit behind it is worth.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT certifies, assesses, verifies and inspects, and explains Understanding certification
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a fixed-price three-year cycle, sector-experienced auditors and one point of contact. Our specialists will tell you what applies to your organisation, what it will take and what it will cost, in one working day.
supportButtons: Buttons: Talk to a specialist (/certification/process) · Talk to a specialist
body: Why it matters to you

The rule shapes what you can ask your certification body for. It can explain the standard, describe the certification process, answer questions about what the audit covers, run training courses, and tell you clearly what the audit found. It cannot write your procedures, carry out your risk assessment, fill your gaps or tell you the specific way to close a nonconformity, because the auditor who then assessed the result would be assessing the body's own work. When a certification body offers to "help you through" implementation as part of the certification package, the certificate it issues may be worth less than you paid for it, and an accredited body will decline. The same separation applies to TRAIBCERT's advisory services in asset management: an organisation that receives system-design advisory from TRAIBCERT is certified by another body, and the engagement letter says so before work starts.
What to do

Use your certification body for what it can do: training, explanation, an honest audit and a clear report. Use your own people, or an independent consultant with no link to the certification body, for implementation. Keep the two in separate contracts, and if anyone offers you both under one roof, ask how the impartiality is protected.

title: ISO 14001:2026 published — transition timetable for certified organisations
excerpt: ISO 14001:2026 was published on 15 April 2026. Certificates to the 2015 edition can be issued until 31 October 2027 and all certified organisations must have transitioned by 30 April 2029.
byline: TRAIBCERT Technical Team · 2026-04-20 · Updated 2026-09-27 · 2 min read
introduction: ISO 14001:2026, the revised environmental management system standard, was published on 15 April 2026 and replaces ISO 14001:2015.
supportTitle: HOW TRAIBCERT SUPPORTS YOU — TRAIBCERT certifies organisations to ISO 14001
supportCopy: As an accredited, independent certification body with a global clientele and an understanding of its clients' needs, TRAIBCERT provides a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit, an independent certification decision and a three-year certificate with annual surveillance. If your certificate or programme is affected by this change, we will plan the response inside your existing cycle at no additional visit.
supportButtons: Buttons: Get a certification quote (/certification/iso-14001) · Talk to a specialist
body: Who is affected

Every organisation certified to ISO 14001:2015 and every organisation planning initial certification. Initial certifications can still be issued to the 2015 edition until 31 October 2027; after that date only the 2026 edition is certified. All existing certificates must be transitioned to the 2026 edition by 30 April 2029, when 2015-edition certificates cease to be valid.
What changed

The structure is unchanged, so existing systems carry over. The revision strengthens the treatment of climate change in the organisation's context and planning, sharpens the expectations on the life-cycle perspective, compliance obligations and the control of outsourced processes, and aligns terminology with the other 2026 management system standards. The changes are proportionate; most certified organisations will find the work concentrated in context, planning and management review.
What to do and by when

Read the transition section of TRAIBCERT's ISO 14001 page, which carries the timeline. Run a gap assessment against the changes using the updated readiness checklist, assign owners, and plan the transition audit to coincide with your next surveillance or recertification visit rather than as an extra. Organisations whose recertification falls before mid-2028 should transition at recertification; those with later dates should transition at a surveillance visit in 2027 or 2028 and not leave it to the final months, when audit dates are scarce.
Where TRAIBCERT stands
TRAIBCERT certifies to ISO 14001:2026 now, combines transition audits with scheduled visits at no additional visit, and can transition a certificate transferred from another body in the same audit.
